events.text: A letter reaches your landing on thin paper, sealed with a smear of wax the colour of a bruise. {sda4_school} has heard of you, it says, and keeps a place. It does not teach what the great academies teach. It teaches what they leave out, and asks no recommendation from anyone. The messenger waits on the cloud-step, chewing a stalk of grass, in no hurry.

choices.text: Accept the place

effects.log: You write one word on the back and hand it over. The messenger nods and is gone before the ink is dry.

choices.text: Send the letter back unopened a second time

effects.log: You return it with a polite line. The messenger shrugs, as if this happened often.

events.text: Nobody invites you to {sda4_school} so much as leave a door open. A rumour at the tea-house, a drifting cloud-pass in your sleeve that you do not remember getting, a stranger who says the term begins at the next new moon. The school has no gate you could point to. It has only a reputation, which is that people go in as one thing and come out as another.

choices.text: Follow the cloud-pass

effects.log: The pass leads you through three cloud-banks to a place that was not on any chart. You take a seat at the back.

choices.text: Burn the pass in a lamp

effects.log: It burns green. You keep to the main road, and wonder for a while.

events.text: A former pupil of {sda4_school} finds you on a ledge of the Sea of Clouds and says, without preamble, that the school remembers promising people. She lists your last three victories correctly, down to the weather. A place is yours if you want it. It will cost no spirit stones, she says, and then looks away, and you understand what that means.

choices.text: Ask what it will cost, then accept

effects.log: She tells you part of it. It is enough. You go.

choices.text: Thank her, and decline

effects.log: She nods as if she expected it, and drops from the ledge into the cloud without a sound.

events.text: The first lessons at {sda4_school} are about forgetting. The masters ask you to unlearn the stance you were proudest of, the greeting you were taught, even how you sit. A classmate with a scarred lip says the trick is to stop apologising for the gaps. By the end of the first month your old habits are in a heap, and something plainer stands where they were.

choices.text: Study the gaps until they close

effects.log: You work through the nights. The gaps do close, and what grows in them is yours.

choices.text: Test the new stance against a classmate

effects.log: You spar until the bell. It is rough, and honest, and somebody laughs afterwards.

choices.text: Learn who teaches what, and who owes whom

effects.log: The school has a ledger no one admits to. By spring you can read it.

events.text: Term-end at {sda4_school} is a contest nobody scheduled. Pupils vanish for a night and return carrying things: a scroll, a bruise, someone else's seal. The masters count them in the morning and say nothing. You are told, by a pupil who is not smiling, that the quiet ones usually do best, and the loud ones usually do the fighting.

choices.text: Spend the night with the old manuals

effects.log: You return with a bruise on your pride and three pages you did not have.

choices.text: Go out and take a seal from someone louder

effects.log: You take one. It is not clean. It is, however, in your sleeve at dawn.

choices.text: Trade something small for something large

effects.log: The trade goes well, and a pupil you will meet again owes you a favour.

events.text: A visiting adept lectures at {sda4_school} for one afternoon, in a room that smells of old tea and wet stone. She says nothing quotable. She walks among the benches and corrects your hands, one by one, in silence, and when she reaches you she holds your wrist a moment longer than the others and says only: slower.

choices.text: Take the word seriously, and practise slowly

effects.log: Slow is harder than fast. It takes the whole season to begin to understand.

choices.text: Challenge her to show you what slow looks like

effects.log: She shows you. You are not the same afterwards, and you are not the first.

choices.text: Ask a classmate what she said to them

effects.log: Everyone was told something different. You collect them like coins.

events.text: Rain on the cloud-roof for nine days. The pupils of {sda4_school} are confined to the long hall, and the hall develops a government. A boy with a loud voice becomes speaker; a quiet girl with a tin whistle becomes judge. You are asked, formally, where you stand. It is the first time in a long while anyone has put the question so plainly.

choices.text: Spend the rain on your studies

effects.log: You are the only one not talking. By the ninth day you have finished a book nobody else opened.

choices.text: Stand against the speaker

effects.log: It is a short, loud affair, and it makes you a few friends and one lasting enemy.

choices.text: Help the quiet judge, and let the speaker think it was his idea

effects.log: The hall settles. You are never thanked, and never forgotten.

events.text: Someone has been leaving small, useful things on your bench at {sda4_school}: a better brush, a folded map, a note of three names. No signature. You suspect two classmates, and a master who has stopped meeting your eye. Whoever it is wants you to be good at this, and wants something, eventually, in return. The generosity has begun to feel like a weight.

choices.text: Use every gift, and learn quickly

effects.log: You learn, and the pace is scary. Whoever is watching is pleased, and does not say so.

choices.text: Leave a note asking them to show themselves

effects.log: The notes go unanswered for a month. Then a hand grips your sleeve in the corridor.

choices.text: Follow the gifts back to the giver

effects.log: It takes patience. The giver is not who you thought, and the reason is stranger.

events.text: The day {sda4_school} lets you go there is no ceremony. A master you rarely spoke to hands you a plain cord, tied in a knot you recognise from the first lesson, and tells you it can be untied by anyone, which is the point. The classmates who remain give you a look that is part envy and part warning. You walk out past the last lamp and do not look at it.

choices.text: Wear the cord openly

effects.log: People ask what the knot is. You tell them a little. It becomes a mark of sorts.

choices.text: Put the cord away, and keep the lessons

effects.log: The cord goes in a box. The lessons stay in your hands.

events.text: You finish at {sda4_school} on an ordinary morning. The long hall is swept, the benches are stacked, and a boy you never liked says goodbye in a voice that suggests he might. The masters write something in a ledger and close it. You carry no certificate, and nothing proves you were ever there, which turns out to be exactly what the school intended.

choices.text: Leave without a word, as the school prefers

effects.log: You go quietly. The road is long and strangely light.

choices.text: Give the boy your best brush

effects.log: He holds it as if it might break. It is the last thing anyone says to you there.

events.text: A voice you half-remember finds you at the mooring: {sda4_school} has not forgotten what it taught you, and would like a favour in return. The favour is small, and specific, and at an awkward hour. It is described, courteously, as a debt of the kind that is only collected once. The speaker adds, almost kindly, that being collected from is better than being forgotten.

choices.text: Pay the favour in full

effects.log: It is as small as promised. When it is done, a door in your memory closes quietly.

choices.text: Refuse, and say the school gave freely

effects.log: The voice says nothing, then laughs once, softly. You are not sure the matter is closed.

events.text: A classmate from {sda4_school} turns up on your doorstep with a hat pulled low and a message: the school is calling in a favour, and you were named. They look tired. They say they were asked to come because nobody else would be believed. If you refuse, they add, it is not they who will be sent next time.

choices.text: Hear them out, and do what is asked

effects.log: You do it. It is not pleasant. The classmate thanks you with a stare at the floor.

choices.text: Send them home with a message of your own

effects.log: The message is short. The classmate reads it twice, and goes.

events.text: A scroll arrives, written in the school's plain hand: a list of what you were taught, and the days you were taught it. At the bottom is one line. It says the account is open. The tone is almost warm. You find you remember every item on the list, and that remembering is how the school keeps its books.

choices.text: Settle the account, once and for all

effects.log: You settle it. The scroll curls and dries in your hand like an old leaf.

choices.text: Tear the scroll, and let the account stay open

effects.log: You tear it. For a long time nothing happens, which is its own kind of waiting.

events.text: A prayer comes to you that is not a prayer: a plain request, whispered at the Gate Shrine in a voice with no name behind it. {sda4_school} keeps a place for you, it says, among gods who have lost their thrones or never had one. There is no tithe and no oath. A cold thread of incense rises from the altar and points, quite clearly, at a door that was not there yesterday.

choices.text: Follow the thread of incense

effects.log: The door opens on a corridor of old lamps. You are expected, and nobody mentions it.

choices.text: Snuff the thread with two fingers

effects.log: The incense dies. The door, if it was ever there, is gone by morning.

events.text: A god without a temple comes to your hall at the hour when offerings are counted. They carry a cup and a satchel and the weary dignity of the unthroned. {sda4_school}, they say, would be glad of you; the lessons are odd, the benches hard, and the company the best in the heavens. They are not selling anything. They are only holding open a door that nobody else will hold.

choices.text: Accept, and ask where the school sits

effects.log: They tell you, and it is somewhere between two domains that disclaim it. You go.

choices.text: Offer the cup back, and decline

effects.log: The god drinks it themselves and departs with great courtesy.

events.text: In the Book of Fates there is a margin, and in the margin there is a note in your own hand that you do not remember writing: attend {sda4_school}. It is dated a thousand years hence, or a thousand years ago. The Keeper of Names says the handwriting is genuine. He also says the note may have been planted by someone who knew you would trust yourself.

choices.text: Trust the note, and go

effects.log: You go. The school is exactly as the note describes, down to the chipped cup.

choices.text: Strike the note out of the margin

effects.log: You strike it out, with a small private pang. The margin stays blank.

events.text: The lessons at {sda4_school} are taught by gods who were taught by gods who are no longer in the Book. The curriculum has no syllabus. On the first day a teacher draws a circle on the floor, steps outside it, and asks the class what is inside. The answers are all wrong. Over the term you come to see that the circle is the lesson, and the wrongness is the way in.

choices.text: Study the circle until it answers

effects.log: It answers, eventually. What it says is not what you expected, and is better.

choices.text: Step into the circle and test the floor

effects.log: The floor holds. A teacher claps once, slowly, and does not smile.

choices.text: Find out who drew the circle first

effects.log: The trail leads to an old rivalry and a broken oath. Knowing it is worth more than the lesson.

events.text: A god of the unfinished crafts lectures at {sda4_school} on how to leave a thing undone so well that it outlives the finished ones. The class takes notes, then discards them. The only note you keep is a doodle of a bridge with the middle missing. A classmate looks at it and says that is the most honest drawing in the room.

choices.text: Study the missing middle

effects.log: You return to it nightly. By the end of term the missing part has begun to make sense.

choices.text: Spar with the classmate who praised it

effects.log: The spar is brief and good-humoured. You both leave with a better understanding of gaps.

choices.text: Trade the drawing for a favour

effects.log: It fetches more than you expected. The favour is yet to be called.

events.text: Fasting week at {sda4_school}: no offerings are accepted, no prayers answered, no worship received. The gods in residence sit in a bare room and are, for seven days, only themselves. Several of them weep. One, a god of harvests, laughs for an hour. You, for your part, notice how much of your hunger was never for food at all.

choices.text: Sit the full week and learn what remains

effects.log: It is a hard week. What remains is small, bright, and entirely your own.

choices.text: Slip away at midnight for a shrine run

effects.log: You return at dawn with offerings in your sleeves. Nobody says anything. Everybody knows.

choices.text: Ration your neighbour's fast for a favour

effects.log: It is cynical, and it works. The god of harvests is grateful beyond reason.

events.text: The graduating class of {sda4_school} puts on a play every year, in which the masterless gods act out the stories of the thrones they never had. You are cast as a minor spirit with one line. The line is a lie. Everyone else's line is a lie too, and the audience applauds the lies as truth. Afterwards a teacher tells you that is the secret of a throne.

choices.text: Learn your line until it is true

effects.log: You learn it, and the truth of it surprises you. The applause is a small, real thing.

choices.text: Improvise a second line

effects.log: The cast freezes, then laughs. The teacher marks you down, and then up.

choices.text: Rewrite the play from the wings

effects.log: You rewrite three scenes. The cast follows the rewrite without noticing.

events.text: Winter in the heavens is a matter of fewer prayers. {sda4_school} goes quiet, and the old stoves are lit in the long gallery. Pupils drift to the stoves and talk, and the talk is the lesson. A fallen god of rains says that falling is a skill like any other. A god without a name says that a name is a thing you borrow. You are given a stool by the fire.

choices.text: Listen all winter, and take notes

effects.log: The notes become a book. It will not be read for centuries.

choices.text: Challenge the fallen god to a game

effects.log: The game is unfair and you lose. You learn a great deal.

choices.text: Trade a secret for a secret by the stove

effects.log: It is a fair trade. You walk away with one you did not expect to want.

events.text: You leave {sda4_school} with nothing in your hands. A teacher walks you to the last arch, the one with no lintel, and says the school's only certificate is that you were admitted to it. The classmates wave from the gallery. Their lamps are still lit; yours is not, quite. You cross the arch and find that your shadow is, for a moment, longer than before.

choices.text: Wear the missing lintel as a mark

effects.log: You tell people about the arch. They think it a riddle. It is.

choices.text: Keep the arch to yourself

effects.log: You tell no one. The arch stays in you, open and unframed.

events.text: Graduation at {sda4_school} is a meal. The masterless and the fallen sit at one long table, the teachers pour, and you are handed a bowl of something plain. When it is eaten, you are done. Several gods embrace you, and one of them presses a small clay figure into your palm that you will not understand for another century. It is warm.

choices.text: Carry the figure everywhere

effects.log: It makes an odd companion. It is also, oddly, correct about weather.

choices.text: Leave the figure at the school's shrine

effects.log: You set it with the others. The shrine seems pleased.

events.text: The School comes to collect. A god in a threadbare robe stands in your Hall of Prayers and says that {sda4_school} gave you something real, and that the gift has a tail. It is a small request: a word in a domain you can reach, a door you can open. It is the kind of thing a graduate does for the school that made them, and it must be done quietly.

choices.text: Do the favour, and be done

effects.log: The word is spoken, the door opened. The god bows and fades, and you feel lighter.

choices.text: Refuse, and say the lessons were free

effects.log: The god says nothing, and then, softly: nothing is. They leave without anger.

events.text: A classmate from {sda4_school} arrives at your altar with a satchel and no incense. They were chosen to ask, they say, because they are the one you would most hate to refuse. The school is calling in its debt. The favour is not dangerous, only awkward. They look at their shoes. You realise it has not got easier for them either.

choices.text: Hear them out, and agree

effects.log: You agree. The favour is awkward, as promised. The classmate cries a little, in relief.

choices.text: Send them home, and say you will think on it

effects.log: You say it kindly. They go. The matter hangs over you like a held breath.

events.text: In the Book of Fates a line appears beneath your name: an account, opened by {sda4_school}, in a hand that is gentle and absolutely firm. It lists every lesson and what it was worth. The sum is not large. It is also not zero. The Keeper of Names asks you privately whether you would like him to pretend he did not see it.

choices.text: Pay the account, as written

effects.log: You pay it. The line fades from the Book, and the Keeper breathes out.

choices.text: Ask him to pretend, and let it stand

effects.log: He pretends. The line stays. It will keep, patient, until it is needed.

events.text: A note in cramped writing is slipped under your door during the night. {sda4_school} has taken an interest in you, it says, and would like to see what you do with a year of its teaching. The school sits off the proper road; you will have to ask the way. No fee is named. A pressed leaf is enclosed, folded small, and is the only seal.

choices.text: Ask the way, and go

effects.log: The way is asked, and answered, and it is longer than you expected. You arrive at dusk.

choices.text: Put the note in the stove

effects.log: The stove takes it without complaint. The leaf curls blue and goes out.

events.text: A pedlar at the market tells you that {sda4_school} remembers you. He says it as if it were weather. You laugh; he does not. He draws a small mark on a scrap of cloth and presses it into your hand: if you find the mark on a gatepost anywhere between here and the coast, that is the door. He adds that the school has not made an exception in years.

choices.text: Keep the cloth, and look for the mark

effects.log: You find it on the third gatepost. The door opens as if it had been waiting.

choices.text: Give the cloth back, and thank him

effects.log: He tucks it away, shrugs, and goes back to selling thread.

events.text: On a road you travel often, a stranger falls into step beside you and talks, lightly, about nothing. At the crossroads, they stop, and say that {sda4_school} could use someone like you. The way they say it is not flattery. It is the plain tone of a person reading from a list. They do not ask for an answer. They only wait to see which fork you take.

choices.text: Take the fork they point to

effects.log: The fork leads down a lane you had never noticed. The school is at the end of it.

choices.text: Take the other fork, and walk on

effects.log: You walk on. The stranger does not follow, and you are almost sorry.

events.text: The first lesson at {sda4_school} is to sit, and listen, and do nothing for an hour. You are sure it is a joke. The teacher is not smiling. After the hour you are asked what you heard, and you realise you heard a great deal: the beams, the draught, the breathing of the pupils, the particular silence of a room where something is being taught. The second hour is harder.

choices.text: Stay in the silence, and learn from it

effects.log: You stay. By the end of the week your ears have changed.

choices.text: Test the teacher with a loud noise

effects.log: The teacher does not blink. You are asked to do it again, quieter, with meaning.

choices.text: Watch which pupils fidget, and when

effects.log: You note them all. It is, you realise, the real lesson.

events.text: A group of pupils from {sda4_school} takes you on a night run through the lower town, along walls and over roofs, past sleeping dogs. It is a game, and also not. You learn where the watch changes and which gate sticks. You learn that the oldest pupil keeps a ledger of every house you passed. You learn that the game is a kind of exam.

choices.text: Study the route until you could run it blind

effects.log: You could, by the end. It is a small, private skill.

choices.text: Race the oldest pupil to the last roof

effects.log: You lose by a hair. They say you ran well, and mean it.

choices.text: Memorise the ledger, and keep it to yourself

effects.log: You do. It is a very good ledger, and it comes in useful.

events.text: The master of {sda4_school} keeps no regular hours. Some mornings they teach until noon; other mornings they are gone, and their lamp burns until midnight with no one in the room. You learn to read the lamp: bright means come, dim means wait, out means leave them. By the second term you can tell what they are thinking from the wick alone.

choices.text: Study the lamp, and its master's moods

effects.log: It is slow learning. It is, however, learning.

choices.text: Go in when the lamp is dim, and ask for a lesson

effects.log: The master looks up with weary eyes and gives you one, short and sharp.

choices.text: Take notes on who is allowed in when

effects.log: The pattern is a map. You keep it close.

events.text: Rain on the roof of {sda4_school}, and an empty yard. A pupil your age sits on the step with a half-eaten apple and tells you, matter-of-factly, that nobody who stays long gets to leave as the same person. They mean it as a warning. They also mean it as a promise. They offer you the other half of the apple.

choices.text: Eat the apple, and ask what they mean

effects.log: It is a long conversation. You come out of it understanding more than you wished.

choices.text: Throw the apple core at the wall, and ask for a bout

effects.log: They laugh. The bout is short and friendly and leaves you both limping.

choices.text: Take the apple, and file the remark away

effects.log: You file it. Later in the year it becomes useful.

events.text: A merchant from the coast pays {sda4_school} a visit and leaves with three pupils, a sack of books and a promise. Nobody explains. The remaining pupils carry on as if a visit of this kind were weather. You ask the oldest what happened and receive a look so dry it could be used to preserve fruit. The school, it seems, sells its pupils sometimes. It prefers to say: places them.

choices.text: Study twice as hard, so you are never placed

effects.log: You study. The merchant does not return for you, though he looks in your direction.

choices.text: Challenge the merchant's favourite to a bout

effects.log: You lose, but it is noticed. The merchant rewrites a line in his book.

choices.text: Find out what the merchant paid

effects.log: The sum is large. It is not as large as the school's debt to him.

events.text: You leave {sda4_school} one grey morning, with a bundle and a loaf. At the gate, the master gives you a short nod and a small clay lamp, unlit, which they say you can light if you ever need to come back. Several pupils line the wall and say goodbye in the offhand way people use when they mean it. You walk down the lane without looking round, and feel the lamp bump against your hip.

choices.text: Carry the lamp openly

effects.log: People ask what it is. You say it is a door. They do not believe you, and are wrong.

choices.text: Pack the lamp away and keep the lessons

effects.log: The lamp sits in your pack. The lessons live in your hands.

events.text: The term at {sda4_school} ends with a meal at a table so long it has to be carried out into the yard. The master serves, the pupils eat, and the stories get progressively less true. At the end a girl who has been silent all year stands and says that she will remember this when she is old. Then she sits, mortified, and everyone cheers. You leave the next day with a full heart and an empty purse.

choices.text: Leave quietly, as the school prefers

effects.log: You go before dawn, with a loaf in each pocket. The road is wide and cool.

choices.text: Press a coin into the silent girl's hand

effects.log: She stares at it, and at you, and smiles for the first time all year.

events.text: A man with a lantern is waiting at your gate one evening. He was sent by {sda4_school}, he says, and he is sorry to be so formal. The school gave you a year, and a year has a price that is not always named at the time. He wants a small thing from you: a word in a certain ear, a door left unlocked on a certain night. He turns the lantern low. Dogs bark somewhere far off.

choices.text: Do the favour the school asks

effects.log: It is done in an evening, quietly. When the night is over, you feel your account go still.

choices.text: Refuse, and tell him the year was fair trade

effects.log: He nods slowly, as if this were the answer he had half expected. He goes without another word.

events.text: An old classmate from {sda4_school} arrives on a mule, dusty and apologetic, and says the school has called in its debts and you are on the list. They were asked to come because they would not be refused. The favour is not dangerous, only awkward, and must be done soon. The mule looks at you with a certain amount of interest.

choices.text: Hear them out, and agree to help

effects.log: You agree. The favour is awkward, as warned. The classmate thanks you on the doorstep and does not stay for tea.

choices.text: Send them off with a loaf and a no

effects.log: You send them off. The mule, at least, seems to approve.

events.text: A letter comes from {sda4_school}, written in a clerk's round hand, listing the year you spent there line by line, with a note at the foot: account open. The tone is mild. It is the kind of mildness that comes from long practice. The letter does not ask for payment. It merely records, and records, and records, until the recording feels like a hand on your shoulder.

choices.text: Pay the account in full, and close it

effects.log: You pay it. The letter in your hand crumbles like old bread.

choices.text: Leave the account open, and carry on

effects.log: You carry on. The letter goes into a drawer and sits there, patient as the school itself.

events.text: The cloud-ferry boy hands you a ticket for a barge that sails on no timetable. The stub bears the stamp of {sda4_school}. "Paid for already," he says, and will not say by whom. The barge is moored at the last pier, lantern lit, one empty bench aboard, its oars already wet.

choices.text: Board the barge

effects.log: The oars dip without a rower. The Isles slide past, and you are the only passenger on the bench.

choices.text: Give the ticket back to the boy

effects.log: He pockets it with a shrug, and the barge leaves empty, still lit.

events.text: Your almanac has grown a star. It sits in the corner of the autumn chart, ringed in red ink you did not use, and beside it a tiny note: {sda4_school}, third watch, the pier with the broken lantern. You check the chart against three others. All of them agree there is a star where there never was.

choices.text: Be at the pier by the third watch

effects.log: The lantern is broken, as promised, and a hand beyond it holds out a lit one.

choices.text: Cross the star out with a brush

effects.log: The ink bleeds into a new shape. You close the almanac on it.

events.text: An old rival catches your sleeve outside the Jade Court and says, quickly and without pride, that {sda4_school} asked her for a name. She gave yours. It was the only honest thing she could think to do for either of you. Now she studies the paving and waits to learn whether she has done you a kindness.

choices.text: Thank her, and go see the school

effects.log: She breathes out. You walk to the school together as far as the first stair.

choices.text: Tell her you would rather choose your own teachers

effects.log: She nods, stiffly, and says she understands. She does not look as though she does.

events.text: On lantern night a paper lantern drifts up through the crowd with a name inked on its belly. It is yours, and under it, in smaller strokes, the name of {sda4_school}. Children point. Nobody else seems troubled. The lantern bobs at the height of your chin, patient, with a small flame that does not flicker in the wind.

choices.text: Catch the lantern and read the rest

effects.log: It carries a map folded in its frame. You follow it, and the crowd closes behind you.

choices.text: Let it float on over the Sea of Clouds

effects.log: It rises until it is a star among stars. You do not see where it goes.

events.text: A clerk of the Lotus Ledger apologises for a mistake. A fee paid in your name has gone to {sda4_school}, and the school, upon receiving it, has entered you on its rolls. The clerk can have it reversed, with forms, in perhaps a decade. In the meantime your bench is warm and your name is on a peg by the door.

choices.text: Let the error stand, and attend

effects.log: The clerk looks relieved. The peg by the door fits your cloak exactly.

choices.text: Insist on the forms

effects.log: The clerk produces them, with the air of someone who has done it before. Years may pass.

events.text: The first exam at {sda4_school} is a storm. Pupils sit on the rail at dawn and must name the hour it breaks over the Sea of Clouds. Most guess. A thin girl in a patched sleeve has been counting gulls since midnight. She writes something down and will not show it. Whatever you write will be marked against hers.

choices.text: Count the gulls, and the cloud-bottoms, and the damp

effects.log: It is slow, dull work, and you are within a quarter-hour. The master marks it down without comment.

choices.text: Stake your reputation aloud on the hour

effects.log: You call it in front of the class. You are wrong by a bell, and right about the room's mood.

choices.text: Sit beside the girl and read her pencil

effects.log: She lets you, with a look that charges for it. You owe her afterwards.

events.text: The pupils of {sda4_school} are set to clean a room. It holds the master's collection of broken sword-hilts, hundreds of them, each tagged in a hand that shakes. No one is told what to do with them. The old master sits among the hilts, drinking tea, and watches who sweeps and who reads the tags.

choices.text: Read every tag, and sweep slowly

effects.log: Each hilt has a name and a reason on its tag. By week's end you know a lot about how things break.

choices.text: Pick up two hilts and test them against each other

effects.log: The master lifts one eyebrow, and then the other. You are asked to leave, politely, for a day.

choices.text: Rearrange them quietly into a better order

effects.log: Someone notices. Someone always does. You are asked to explain, and your answer is overheard.

events.text: Fog on the Sea of Clouds. {sda4_school} sends its pupils out in a barge with no lantern and one rule: bring it back without scraping a pier. The oarsman is blindfolded. The pupils whisper. Somewhere a bell tolls, flat, and no one can say from which side. You hold the tiller, since nobody else will.

choices.text: Steer by the bell and the feel of the current

effects.log: It takes all night. You touch the pier at dawn so lightly it barely rocks.

choices.text: Ram on through, trusting the barge to the Isles

effects.log: You scrape the pier with a groan of timber. Everyone cheers anyway.

choices.text: Trade places with the oarsman for his bearings

effects.log: He mutters what he remembers. It is more than he meant to say.

events.text: A pupil of {sda4_school} is caught copying pages from the Jade Court's archive. The long hall splits over what to do. The masters sit in a row and say nothing, which the pupils take for permission to argue. By evening you have been asked, by both sides, to speak. The accused sits on the bench, small and straight.

choices.text: Argue from the archive's own rules, line by line

effects.log: It is a dry speech and it works. The hall quiets, and the masters take notes.

choices.text: Shout down the loudest accuser

effects.log: It is not elegant. The accused looks at you with astonished gratitude.

choices.text: Offer the accused a place among your own contacts

effects.log: He accepts, quickly. A favour is born in the dark of the long hall.

events.text: At {sda4_school} each pupil is told to argue the position they find most repugnant, for a full evening, with the masters as judges. You draw a slip. It is the position of the faction that raised you. The room goes quiet as the other pupils realise whose name is on the slip, and begin to wait.

choices.text: Argue it as well as it can be argued

effects.log: You find, to your discomfort, that it has real strengths. You come away humbler.

choices.text: Argue it badly on purpose and be caught

effects.log: The masters catch it at once. The lesson is not the one you meant to give.

choices.text: Argue it so well your own side is the one embarrassed

effects.log: It travels. Weeks later, someone quotes you to you.

events.text: The roof-garden of {sda4_school} withers in a week. Nobody speaks of poison, which is how everyone knows. The masters, haggard, set the pupils to digging up the beds. At the bottom of the third you find a clay seal you recognise from a rival academy, grey with damp, and turn it over in your fingers.

choices.text: Wash and record the seal, and bring it to the masters

effects.log: They listen. The garden is replanted, and the rival's name is not spoken for a while.

choices.text: Confront the rival academy's pupils in the courtyard

effects.log: It ends in a shoving match. Their leader swears they did not do it, and you half believe her.

choices.text: Keep the seal, and watch who asks for it

effects.log: Three people ask in a week. The list is useful in ways you did not foresee.

events.text: A hermit master of {sda4_school} sleeps through his own lectures. The pupils take turns copying down whatever he mutters, and compare notes after. The notes disagree. Eventually someone realises he is correcting exactly the mistakes the pupils would make that week. The listening becomes, quietly, the whole course.

choices.text: Copy every word and study them as a cycle

effects.log: The cycle holds. By midwinter you can finish his sentences, and sometimes his thoughts.

choices.text: Wake him with a question

effects.log: He opens one eye, answers it, and goes back to sleep. The whole class is jealous.

choices.text: Sell your notes to the next year's pupils

effects.log: They fetch more than you expected, and a reputation you did not intend.

events.text: The senior pupils of {sda4_school} invite the new year to a kite contest above the Isles. The rule is simple: cut the others' strings. The kites are lacquered, the strings ground glass and rice-paste. Some pupils treat it as a joke. Others have been practising for months. The wind turns north, and the first string parts with a small sound.

choices.text: Fly low and steady, and let the others tangle

effects.log: Your kite is the last in the air. The wind approves of patience.

choices.text: Go straight at the seniors' best kite

effects.log: You lose the kite and win the seniors' respect, which is not nothing.

choices.text: Offer a pact to three other flyers against the leader

effects.log: The pact holds just long enough. Afterwards, nobody quite trusts anyone.

events.text: A silent month at {sda4_school}: no speech in the halls, none at the table, none in the baths. The pupils drift into signs and notes. By the second week the school has developed a tiny, elaborate language of eyebrows. A master leaves tea at your door each morning, unlabelled, and appears to want you to notice.

choices.text: Use the silence to practise stillness

effects.log: The quiet becomes a room you can walk into whenever you like.

choices.text: Break the silence once, at full volume, on the roof

effects.log: You are not punished. The master leaves two cups of tea the next morning.

choices.text: Learn the eyebrow-language, and read the whole hall

effects.log: You learn who is in love, who is in debt, and who is leaving.

events.text: An inspector from the Celestial Ministries arrives at {sda4_school} on a polished barge. The masters hide the real curriculum under a decoy timetable, and the pupils are told to recite lines about harmony. The inspector asks a child what she learned that week. The hall holds its breath around the child.

choices.text: Coach the child gently before she answers

effects.log: She says exactly the safe thing, and means it. The inspector leaves content.

choices.text: Step forward and answer for the whole school

effects.log: The inspector looks at you for a long while. The school is not shut, and not forgotten.

choices.text: Slip the inspector's steward a good report to deliver

effects.log: The report is delivered. The steward remembers who wrote it.

events.text: A pupil's mother arrives at {sda4_school} on the weekly barge, with dumplings and a basket of dried plums. She is mortal-born, and cannot find which stair leads where, and her son hides behind a pillar. The hall pretends not to see. The plums are, you find, extraordinarily good, and she is looking for someone to eat them.

choices.text: Sit with her, and eat, and ask about the village

effects.log: She tells you the village songs. Her son comes out from the pillar eventually.

choices.text: Tell the hall to stop whispering

effects.log: The hall stops. The mother never learns why the stairs were so quiet.

choices.text: Ask where the plums are grown, and who might sell them

effects.log: A modest, useful trade is born over dumplings.

events.text: The master of {sda4_school} vanishes for a week, leaving an envelope on her desk marked "if I do not return". The senior pupils argue whether to open it. A younger pupil already has, and put it back, and wears the stricken face of someone who did. Everyone watches you to see which way the school will go.

choices.text: Hold the school to its routine until she returns

effects.log: She returns on the seventh day, tired. She asks who kept the bells, and you do not say.

choices.text: Demand the younger pupil say what the envelope held

effects.log: The pupil weeps and tells. It was only a recipe, and an apology.

choices.text: Offer to read the envelope aloud, if the hall agrees

effects.log: The hall agrees. You read it carefully, and everyone is changed by it, a little.

events.text: A cloud-beast calf hatches in the dormitory of {sda4_school}, wet and furious, from an egg that was meant for the master's kitchen. The calf imprints on whoever is nearest, which is you. Fifty pupils and three teachers now look at the creature clinging to your sleeve, and at you, and wait.

choices.text: Learn how to raise it from the old books

effects.log: The calf thrives. The books were right about most things, and wrong about the rest.

choices.text: Defend the calf from the kitchen staff

effects.log: You win a loud argument. The calf sleeps on your pillow after.

choices.text: Let the teachers think it was their idea to keep it

effects.log: They think so. The school gains a mascot, and you gain a quiet ally.

events.text: The stairs of {sda4_school} have a rule: nobody may speak the name of a person leaving the school until a year after they are gone. This term a favourite pupil is expelled. Their name hangs unsaid in every room. Their bench is bare, their lamp still warm. You are the only one who saw what really happened.

choices.text: Write down what you saw, and seal it for later

effects.log: The record sits in a drawer, waiting for the year to turn.

choices.text: Speak the name aloud in the long hall

effects.log: There is a long hush. Nobody punishes you, and nobody thanks you.

choices.text: Tell the expelled pupil, quietly, who to thank

effects.log: The pupil's letter reaches you a month later, on very good paper.

events.text: A blizzard of cherry petals buries the courtyard of {sda4_school} three days before the winter exams. The petals are not from any tree on the Isles. The masters call it a nuisance. A wind-sage in the east wing calls it a message. The pupils spend a day sweeping, and a night reading the pattern the petals fell in.

choices.text: Map the pattern on paper and study it

effects.log: The map resembles nothing you know, but it keeps drawing your eye.

choices.text: Sweep it into a heap and set it alight

effects.log: It burns with a sweet smoke. Several pupils feel faint, and cheerfully so.

choices.text: Sell small bags of the petals to the younger pupils

effects.log: They go quickly. You are asked later what the petals do. You say, truthfully, that you do not know.

events.text: On your last day at {sda4_school} the long hall is empty except for a single cushion, set squarely in the middle. A master tells you that you may sit on it or step around it, and that the school will think no worse of you either way. The hall waits to see which you do. Outside, the cloud-bell tolls twice.

choices.text: Sit for one breath, and rise

effects.log: The cushion is warm from the last pupil. You rise lighter than you sat.

choices.text: Step around it and out the door

effects.log: The door shuts gently behind you. Someone laughs, kindly, inside.

events.text: A younger pupil of {sda4_school} follows you to the pier with a bundle in both hands. They wrapped your three favourite brushes, and a pot of ink, and a slip of paper with ten questions on it. They ask you to answer, someday, by whatever road reaches them. The ferry horn sounds. They do not look at the ferry.

choices.text: Take the bundle, and promise an answer

effects.log: You promise, and mean it. The ferry takes a long time to leave.

choices.text: Answer the first question on the spot

effects.log: You answer one aloud on the pier. Nine remain, and you will think of them.

events.text: The master of {sda4_school} does not attend your leaving. A tray is left outside your door instead: tea, three plain cakes, and a single blank sheet of paper. A note says to write the one thing you learned. You turn the paper over twice. The tea cools. The cakes are, as ever, a little stale and entirely sufficient.

choices.text: Write the one thing, and leave the sheet on the tray

effects.log: You write it. Years later you cannot recall the word, but you remember writing it.

choices.text: Leave it blank, and eat the cakes

effects.log: Blank is also an answer. You eat all three cakes, and leave a clean tray.

events.text: As you leave {sda4_school}, the pupils line the stair and each hold out one thing: a ribbon, a stone, a pressed leaf, a folded joke. It is the school's custom. You are handed some thirty small, odd things. By the last step you are carrying a loose, rattling bundle that smells of ink, rain and cheap sweets.

choices.text: Wear one of each, wherever you go

effects.log: You look absurd. People remember you, and ask, and you tell them.

choices.text: Keep them in a box and open it on bad days

effects.log: The box is a small, private weather. It helps more often than not.

events.text: A moth lands on your cup, and in the moth's wings is a faint script: {sda4_school} would like a return of favour, small and tidy, within the month. The script gives a place, an hour, and a name. You recognise the name. It belongs to someone you have no reason to like. The moth waits on the rim, wings folded, until you decide.

choices.text: Go to the place, and do what is asked

effects.log: The favour is as tidy as promised. The moth flies off, and the cup is still warm.

choices.text: Brush the moth away

effects.log: It flutters up and out of the window. The script on the cup fades, slowly.

events.text: The school's old porter finds you on the White Stairs, leaning on a broom. {sda4_school} remembers, he says, in the tone of one passing on a weather report. He lists three small things that are needed and one that is not small. You may choose which to do. He adds, apologetic, that the large one is the one they would prefer.

choices.text: Do the large one

effects.log: It is large. It takes a season and some pride, and the porter blesses you at the end.

choices.text: Do the three small ones, and decline the large

effects.log: The porter nods, writes something down, and says it will do. It does not quite.

events.text: A student of the year below you at {sda4_school} comes to your landing with a petition signed by half the pupils. It asks for a favour, and says you will recognise the sort. The school itself does not demand it, only hopes. The petition is very well written. The signatures are in a dozen hands, some of them shaky.

choices.text: Grant the favour, for the pupils' benefit

effects.log: It is hard, and you are glad afterwards. Some of the signers send you tea.

choices.text: Decline, and tell them to learn to ask in their own names

effects.log: They go, disappointed and thoughtful. One of them looks back.

events.text: A pilgrim kneels at your shrine and leaves, as an offering, a clay tablet with no prayer on it. It bears only the seal of {sda4_school}. The pilgrim does not ask for anything. When you turn the tablet over, there is a place scratched for you at the long table, a bowl, a mat, and the hour the lamps are lit.

choices.text: Keep the tablet, and take the mat

effects.log: The scratch matches your hand exactly. You go that evening, and the lamps are lit.

choices.text: Return the tablet to the offering bowl

effects.log: The bowl swallows it with a soft chime. The pilgrim is gone from the steps.

events.text: Your festival day is spoiled by a minor god who arrives uninvited, stands in the incense, and talks about {sda4_school} for a quarter hour without ever quite saying what it is. He praises its cooking. He praises its drains. Only as he leaves does he mention, as an afterthought, that a bowl has been put aside for you.

choices.text: Ask him the way

effects.log: He draws it in the ash of your censer. It is shorter than you expected.

choices.text: Thank him for his time and turn back to the rite

effects.log: He shrugs, glances back once, and the incense swallows him.

events.text: A dream: you sit in an empty hall and a voice reads your prayers back to you, the ones no one else has heard. When it finishes it names {sda4_school} and falls silent. You wake with the taste of cold tea. In the morning your altar bears one small, unlit lamp that you did not put there.

choices.text: Light the lamp and follow its smoke

effects.log: The smoke trails northwards. You follow it past three domains before it thins.

choices.text: Pinch out the wick and sleep another night

effects.log: The lamp is gone by noon. The dream does not return.

events.text: In the Book of Fates, beside your name, a hand has pencilled a single word: school. No one in the Court of Scribes will admit to it. A scribe, under pressure, concedes that {sda4_school} has the right to annotate any god's entry that it thinks it can teach. Your margin glows faintly with an invitation.

choices.text: Pencil your answer under the word

effects.log: The ink dries. A messenger appears, bows, and escorts you out by a side stair.

choices.text: Ask the scribes to rub it out

effects.log: They do, with a long face. The margin stays slightly paler there.

events.text: Your high priest announces, nervously, that a delegation from {sda4_school} waits in the lower court. They carry no gifts, wear no insignia and speak in the plural. They would like you to look at their students' work. The priest is shaking. The delegation is perfectly pleasant and refuses all offers of refreshment.

choices.text: Receive them, and look at the work

effects.log: The work is odd and fine. You promise to visit the school, and mean it.

choices.text: Receive them, and say your calendar is full

effects.log: They take it gracefully, and the priest's hands stop shaking.

events.text: A god of the lost-and-found lectures at {sda4_school} for a morning, and sets a task: each student must return something to someone who does not know it was missing. The students scatter into the heavens. You find a lock of hair, a half-sung tune, a boundary stone. Which of them do you try to return first?

choices.text: Take the tune, and hunt patiently for its owner

effects.log: It takes weeks. At the end an old goddess weeps to hear it, and thanks no one.

choices.text: Take the boundary stone, and set it back by force of will

effects.log: The stone grinds home. A neighbouring god files a complaint.

choices.text: Take the lock of hair, and find out whose it is by asking quietly around

effects.log: It belonged to a minor spirit. The favour of a minor spirit is, you learn, long-lived.

events.text: Silence is the subject at {sda4_school} this term: the unanswered prayer. The masters read out petitions that were never granted, one after another, without comment, for hours. A girl in the front row begins to cry. The teacher does not stop. At the end each student is asked what they would have done instead.

choices.text: Write out a careful answer for the worst of them

effects.log: You write for two nights. The page is read in class, and nobody speaks after.

choices.text: Say aloud that the silence was cruel

effects.log: The master hears you out. They say that is the right anger, and ask what you will do with it.

choices.text: Take notes on which petitions were ignored by whom

effects.log: The list is long. It contains some surprising names, and a few you can use.

events.text: {sda4_school} sends its students to hold a minor vigil at a failing shrine. The shrine is small, its god long gone, its offerings reduced to a cracked bowl. Three nights are required. On the second, a mortal child wanders in, sits down, and starts talking to the empty altar as though someone were there.

choices.text: Listen as the god would have listened

effects.log: You listen all night. By dawn the child sleeps, and something in the altar glows briefly.

choices.text: Chase away the other students who are laughing

effects.log: They go, shamefaced. The child never notices.

choices.text: Note down every request the child makes, and pass them to a better-placed god

effects.log: Three are answered by week's end. The child never knows who to thank.

events.text: A fast is declared at {sda4_school}: no offerings accepted, no incense burned, no hymns sung, for forty days. The students grow thin and clear-eyed. The masters watch, and eat nothing in front of them. In the fourth week a rich worshipper leaves a platter of sweet cakes at the door, with a note that says only: for the hungry.

choices.text: Leave the cakes untouched and keep the fast

effects.log: The cakes harden on the step. You grow lighter, and see farther.

choices.text: Carry the platter back to the worshipper

effects.log: The worshipper sits, astonished, a long while. The platter is accepted at last.

choices.text: Offer to share the cakes quietly among the youngest

effects.log: The youngest are fed. The masters never mention it.

events.text: The temple clocks at {sda4_school} run wrong by a different amount in every hall, and the students are expected to compensate. Late for the same lesson three days running, you realise the lateness is itself the lesson. A master peers at you over her glasses and asks what hour it really is. There are many wrong answers.

choices.text: Compare all the clocks and compute the true hour

effects.log: You do it in a notebook. The master takes it away and reads it with her tea.

choices.text: Smash the loudest clock

effects.log: The master sighs, and charges you for it in chores. The loud clock is much missed.

choices.text: Sell the correct hour to students who are late

effects.log: Business is brisk. The master discovers it and looks almost proud.

events.text: A student at {sda4_school} claims to have been a god of rain before the Court reassigned them. Nobody believes this, and nobody can disprove it. The claim is put to a trial: the student is to make it rain on the roof for ten minutes, in front of everyone. The sky is clear. Everybody leans in.

choices.text: Study the clouds, and help where the weather allows

effects.log: A shower arrives, thin and late. The student says that is about right.

choices.text: Heckle, loudly, to see whether they crack

effects.log: They do not. The rain starts anyway, from a very small cloud right over your head.

choices.text: Quietly bribe a real rain-spirit to oblige

effects.log: The rain obliges, handsomely. The student never learns who helped.

events.text: At {sda4_school}, apprentices serve a term at the incense-furnace, feeding it herbs by weight. The furnace has an opinion, and delivers it in smoke. Today it reeks of something burnt-sweet and sad. The master of the furnace says a god, somewhere, is losing their faith, and the furnace can smell it. She asks who will go.

choices.text: Go, and sit with the doubting god

effects.log: The god is a small thing in a poor shrine. You stay a week and say very little.

choices.text: Go, and demand they pull themselves together

effects.log: The god weeps, then glares, then laughs. It is not what you planned, and it works.

choices.text: Go, and trade them a patron who will pay for faith

effects.log: The deal is arranged. It is good business and a little sad.

events.text: The students of {sda4_school} put on a play for the heavenly kitchens, with real gods in the audience. It is a farce about a god who loses his temple and finds it in a teapot. The lead has fallen ill. You are the understudy. The curtain is in ten minutes, and the kitchen gods have already started to heckle.

choices.text: Learn the lines from the prompter in the interval

effects.log: You are word-perfect by the second act. The laughter is warm.

choices.text: Walk on and improvise, and shove the heckler off his stool

effects.log: The heckler lands in a basket of rice. The audience adores it.

choices.text: Cut a deal with the stagehands to feed you cues

effects.log: They cue you superbly. You owe them each a favour, one for every scene.

events.text: A visiting inquisitor lectures at {sda4_school} on the weighing of souls. The inquisitor is dry and precise, and brings a set of tiny brass scales. Each student must weigh a made-up soul, justify the weight, and defend it against questions. You draw a soul described only as: a baker who gave away bread and cheated at cards.

choices.text: Set out the loaves and cards in two honest pans

effects.log: The scales settle. The inquisitor nods, once, and writes a figure.

choices.text: Argue that the cards weigh nothing against the bread

effects.log: The inquisitor argues back with relish. You lose well, and learn.

choices.text: Find out what the baker actually wanted, and weigh that

effects.log: It tips the scales entirely. The inquisitor puts away the brass and stares.

events.text: The kitchen god of {sda4_school} teaches the students how a feast is set: who sits where, who is served first, whose cup is filled. It is clearly a lesson in rank, and every student pretends it is a lesson in cooking. The old god tastes your soup, pauses, and tells you it needs more salt, and more courage.

choices.text: Cook it again until the soup is right

effects.log: The third batch is nearly perfect. The old god takes a second bowl.

choices.text: Throw the first batch at the loudest critic

effects.log: It misses, and hits the cook. You wash pots for a week and are not unhappy.

choices.text: Learn which guest is allergic to what, and who takes offence at what

effects.log: The list is a treasure. You sell none of it, and use all of it.

events.text: A student at {sda4_school} has stolen a minor blessing from the shrine of a neighbouring god and swears they did not. The accused is a quiet, sad person who flinches when spoken to. The students form a ring. A small quiet voice asks you to speak for the accused. The ring waits.

choices.text: Examine the blessing's trail, and show where it truly went

effects.log: It led to a mortal baby's cradle. The ring melts, embarrassed.

choices.text: Stand in front of the accused and say let them be

effects.log: The ring grumbles and breaks. The accused will not meet your eye for a month, and then does.

choices.text: Persuade the neighbouring god to quietly forgive it

effects.log: The god shrugs and says it was never missed. The accused weeps.

events.text: A fortnight of rain in the heavenly gardens, and {sda4_school} gives its students a day in a hall of ancestors to dry off and be properly bored. On one wall a thousand names; on another, a thousand blank spaces. A guard at the door mentions casually that your name is among the blank ones and gives you chalk.

choices.text: Write nothing, and study the thousand names instead

effects.log: By dusk you know who is who in the hall. It was the point.

choices.text: Scribble your name in the biggest space

effects.log: The guard laughs. It lasts until the next rain.

choices.text: Copy the names, and swap a few with their neighbours

effects.log: No one notices for a year, which tells you something about halls.

events.text: The students of {sda4_school} must each adopt a mortal prayer for a season and answer it in their own style. Yours is a farmer's, for a late frost. The farmer wants it gone. The frost has its own opinion, and a certain claim: it is saving the seed from rot. You are trying to decide whom you work for.

choices.text: Move the frost gently, bit by bit, over weeks

effects.log: The seed thrives, the farmer is none the wiser, and the frost is satisfied.

choices.text: Drive the frost off at once, and be shouted at by its patron

effects.log: The patron shouts. The farmer's field blooms. You swallow the scolding.

choices.text: Find the farmer a different way to save the seed

effects.log: It takes bartering with a barn-spirit. The farmer sleeps soundly.

events.text: A master of {sda4_school} gives the students a riddle on the first day of winter and disappears for the season. The riddle: what does a god owe the first one who ever prayed to them? Students argue in the dormitory, in the bath-house, in the chapel. The riddle grows an enormous, gossipy skin of theories.

choices.text: Spend the season in quiet thought

effects.log: The answer you arrive at is plainer than the others. It is also truer.

choices.text: Challenge the loudest theory-monger to a debate

effects.log: The debate is long and rude and good. Both of you change your minds.

choices.text: Collect every theory, and publish them with commentary

effects.log: The pamphlet circulates through three heavens. The master reads it, smiling.

events.text: At {sda4_school} you are handed, on leaving, a very ordinary bowl. It has a small chip at the rim. A master says that it has been used by every graduate before you, and that none have thrown it away. You turn it over: beneath, in many tiny scratches, are initials. Yours goes last. The bowl is surprisingly heavy.

choices.text: Carry the bowl to your temple, and use it for offerings

effects.log: The chipped bowl becomes a minor relic. Pilgrims touch it for luck.

choices.text: Leave it at the school with your initials, for the next

effects.log: The master smiles and sets it on the shelf with the others.

events.text: The graduating gods of {sda4_school} are each given a single instruction to carry out in the heavens before the next solstice. Yours is: be kind to a stranger in a way that costs you something. No further detail. You sit on the steps outside with the scroll in your lap, wondering how to find the stranger, and what it will cost.

choices.text: Wait for the stranger to appear, and be ready

effects.log: They arrive soon enough, in a patched robe, asking the way. You walk them there yourself.

choices.text: Go out and seek one deliberately

effects.log: The seeking costs you a whole week. You find them, and they decline help, and it still counts.

events.text: On your last evening at {sda4_school} the cook fills a lacquered box with food for the road: dried figs, a flat cake, a boiled egg stamped with the school's seal. The box is for a long journey, he says. You protest that gods do not eat. He says only that the egg is for hope, and the figs for patience, and the cake for the rest.

choices.text: Eat the egg on the road, and feel hopeful

effects.log: It is a very good egg. You leave the shell on a shrine step.

choices.text: Save the box unopened

effects.log: You keep it on your altar. It never goes stale.

events.text: The final lesson at {sda4_school} is held without a teacher. The students sit in a ring in the dusk and each speaks, in turn, one thing they will no longer do. The ring is long. Some answers are funny, some are heavy. Yours is next. A hush falls, and the lamps burn low on their wicks.

choices.text: Speak truly, and be heard

effects.log: You say it. The ring is quiet, then answers with a single soft word.

choices.text: Make a joke of it, and receive a laugh

effects.log: The laugh is kind. Later, alone, you find you meant it more than you showed.

events.text: A letter of thanks arrives at your temple from {sda4_school}, expensively sealed, with a marginal note in a hand you remember: could you perhaps just once do the school a service. The service is described in careful, mild language, and is in fact sizeable. A priest at your elbow reads over your shoulder and whistles.

choices.text: Perform the service, and be done

effects.log: It is long and tiresome, and when done the school sends a bowl of rice, which is enough.

choices.text: Reply that the school's teaching was its own reward

effects.log: The reply is read, and an eyebrow, somewhere, lifts.

events.text: A former classmate presents themselves at your altar as a petitioner, humbly, and asks for a boon on behalf of {sda4_school}. Their eyes say the school asked them to be this humble. The boon is nothing special: a word in the Court of Scribes. They kneel on the stone, miserable, and wait.

choices.text: Grant the boon, and lift them to their feet

effects.log: The word is spoken, the matter eased. The classmate walks out looking ten years younger.

choices.text: Decline the boon, and offer a chair instead

effects.log: You offer tea. The classmate takes it, quiet, and goes home with nothing else.

events.text: In the Book of Fates a small note has appeared in the margin of your day: owed to {sda4_school}, one favour, of its choosing. The note is signed with the school's mark and a drawing of an owl. It does not specify a date. It simply sits there, like a pebble in a shoe, waiting to be mentioned.

choices.text: Seek out the school and offer to pay at once

effects.log: The school is surprised, then pleased. The favour is quick and the margin is clear.

choices.text: Ignore the note, and hope the owl forgets

effects.log: The owl does not forget. The note remains, a patient, faint grey.

events.text: A ferryman who has never spoken to you before hands you your change and a folded square of reed paper. It carries the mark of {sda4_school}, and one line: the next boat leaves from the reeds, not the pier. He looks at the river and hums, as if he had not just passed on a secret. The reed paper smells faintly of woodsmoke.

choices.text: Wait for the boat in the reeds

effects.log: It comes at dusk, poled by a girl of ten. She does not ask your name.

choices.text: Fold the paper small and drop it in the river

effects.log: The current takes it. The ferryman does not look round.

events.text: The old woman next door, in the middle of a story about a goat, stops and tells you that {sda4_school} asked after you at the well. The old woman says it casually, stirring soup, and goes on with the goat. When the soup is done she adds that the school pays in lessons and not in coin, and you may go or not as you please.

choices.text: Ask her where the school keeps its door

effects.log: She tells you. It turns out to be three streets from your own.

choices.text: Pretend you did not hear, and ask about the goat

effects.log: She gives you the end of the goat story, and a very small smile.

events.text: At the end of the harvest fair a travelling tinker sets out a tray of tiny carved door-keys and tells every passer-by that one will fit. When you pick up the brass one, he leans in and says {sda4_school}. Nothing more. The key is warm from his hand and fits the palm exactly. Other customers drift away.

choices.text: Pay a copper for the key and ask where it fits

effects.log: He tells you the lane and the hour. The lock is under a fig tree.

choices.text: Put the key back on the tray

effects.log: He wraps it in a rag and turns to the next customer.

events.text: Rumour in the grain market is that {sda4_school} takes one pupil a year from each town and has not yet taken one from yours. The sellers wink at you over their sacks. A boy sweeping up chaff says, flatly, that it will be someone who can keep a secret. He glances at you, then at the ground.

choices.text: Ask the boy what the school wants of a pupil

effects.log: He tells you, haltingly, and then disappears into the crowd.

choices.text: Buy a sack of millet and go home

effects.log: The millet is good. The rumour follows you down the lane.

events.text: {sda4_school} sends its pupils to the market with a single copper and a single instruction: come back with a story that is worth more. Stalls steam in the cold. A cobbler sells you a tale for the copper; a weaver offers a better one if you will carry her loom. A thin boy has already come back, empty-handed, with a smile.

choices.text: Listen to every seller, and buy the best

effects.log: The best tale cost a copper and an afternoon, and is told for years.

choices.text: Haul the weaver's loom for her story

effects.log: It is heavy, and the tale is good. Your shoulders ache for three days.

choices.text: Sell the cobbler's tale to the weaver for her own

effects.log: Both are delighted. You come home with a story and a pair of mended soles.

events.text: An autumn flood cuts the road to {sda4_school} and strands the pupils in a drovers' inn for a week. The masters, soaked, hold lessons in the taproom. The innkeeper charges by the candle. A pedlar sleeps on the bench through all of it, snoring. By the fifth day the school has reorganised itself round the hearth.

choices.text: Take notes on every lesson, and mark the pedlar's snores in the margin

effects.log: The notes are rich. The pedlar becomes a small legend.

choices.text: Win the bench by the fire in a game of knucklebones

effects.log: You hold the bench for two days. Then you give it to a shivering teacher.

choices.text: Strike a deal with the innkeeper for a cheaper candle

effects.log: You do. The whole school profits and half of it thanks you.

events.text: A drought in the valley and {sda4_school} is asked to help dig a channel from the river to the dry fields. The pupils are issued mattocks. The masters pick up mattocks too, with great dignity. The work is hot and dull. A farmer's wife brings sour milk at noon and watches the line of sweating scholars.

choices.text: Dig steadily, and learn how water wants to move

effects.log: By week's end you can read a slope like a book.

choices.text: Out-dig the biggest farm lad, for the honour of the school

effects.log: You do. He shakes your hand, and then drops the mattock and weeps with exhaustion.

choices.text: Organise the line into shifts, and trade rest for water

effects.log: The channel is done in half the time. The wife asks who thought of that.

events.text: A strange pupil joins {sda4_school} halfway through the term, a tall person in a hooded cloak who says nothing and sits at the back. They eat standing up. They write with their left hand and read with their right. The masters seem to expect them. By the fourth week half the class has a theory about who they are.

choices.text: Ask them politely about their studies

effects.log: They answer in a handful of dry words. It is more than anyone else has got.

choices.text: Challenge them to a bout, to see what they are

effects.log: They accept with a bow. The bout is shorter than you planned and more instructive.

choices.text: Tail them home, and find out where they sleep

effects.log: It is a haystack. You say nothing, and they leave you a bun on your bench.

events.text: At {sda4_school} a pupil is chosen each month to be Silent Host: they say nothing for a day, and serve the rest. It is your turn. You carry trays, pour tea, wipe benches, and are ignored by everyone as though you were furniture. It is astonishing what people say in front of furniture.

choices.text: Listen only, and serve with grace

effects.log: By evening you know the hearts of a dozen classmates. You keep every word.

choices.text: Drop a tray on the loudest gossip

effects.log: The tray rings like a gong. The gossip stops. You are forgiven by supper.

choices.text: Remember who said what, and to whom

effects.log: The list is invaluable. You will not spend it, but you will keep it.

events.text: A travelling troupe of acrobats camps beside {sda4_school} for a month, and the pupils sneak out to watch. The troupe's leader, a broad woman with a gold tooth, notices and offers to teach a few tricks for an afternoon. The masters pretend not to see the pupils vault the wall.

choices.text: Study her balance, and copy it slowly

effects.log: You find a point of calm in your hips you never knew. The woman winks.

choices.text: Spar with her tumblers, fall hard, and laugh

effects.log: You are bruised head to foot, and grinning.

choices.text: Persuade the masters to host the troupe in the hall

effects.log: They are scandalised and then delighted. The troupe stays the winter.

events.text: The master of {sda4_school} announces an unannounced exam, to be held whenever the bell next rings, which it does not do for eleven days. The pupils grow thin with watchfulness. On the twelfth morning the bell rings, and the exam is to describe what you did on the days before. The ink is already drying on your neighbour's page.

choices.text: Describe the eleven days honestly and in detail

effects.log: The master reads it twice and says it is the only true answer.

choices.text: Refuse to write until you know the marking

effects.log: The master smiles and sets you outside, to think. You think.

choices.text: Copy the neighbour's opening and improve on it

effects.log: The master notes the copy and the improvement. Both go in the register.

events.text: A pupil of {sda4_school} is ill with fever, and the school's custom is for the whole year to take turns by the sickbed. Your watch is the small hours. The patient talks in their sleep, about a sister, a river, a debt of eight silver pieces. At dawn they wake and ask what they said. They watch your face.

choices.text: Tell them a part, and keep the rest to yourself

effects.log: They breathe out, and press your hand. You speak of it to nobody.

choices.text: Tell them it was nonsense, and mean it

effects.log: They believe you, and are kinder to you for the rest of the term.

choices.text: Tell them everything, and offer to carry the debt

effects.log: They are silent, then furious, then grateful. A friendship is born, unevenly.

events.text: A bell-founder comes to {sda4_school} to cast a new bell for the school, and the pupils are asked to help with the moulds. It is hot, sooty work. The founder insists the bell is only as good as the hands that built the clay around it. After the pour, nobody speaks until it cools and rings, a deep note, slightly off, and perfect.

choices.text: Stay to the end, and listen to the cooling

effects.log: The note shifts slightly as the metal settles. You will recognise it anywhere.

choices.text: Lift the clay mould from the pit with your own back

effects.log: It is the heaviest thing you have lifted. The founder pats your shoulder.

choices.text: Offer to sell the bell's offcuts as keepsakes

effects.log: The school clears a few pennies. The founder is amused.

events.text: On the last day at {sda4_school}, the cook presses a loaf of bread into your hands, still hot, wrapped in cloth. She says nothing. She has fed three generations of pupils and never once been thanked. She watches you take it, and then goes back into the kitchen, wiping her hands on her apron. The bread is better than anything the masters taught.

choices.text: Eat it on the road, and think of her

effects.log: It lasts a day. You think of her for much longer.

choices.text: Go back and thank her properly

effects.log: She flaps a hand, red-faced. You are given a second loaf.

events.text: The pupils of {sda4_school} leave in the same order they entered, by the reeds and the ferry and the long lane to the road. The ferry is crowded. A mother with a basket sits beside you and asks what you studied. You open your mouth and discover that you cannot say it in a sentence, which is, you suppose, the point.

choices.text: Tell her three small things you learned

effects.log: She nods at each. She knows a fourth, and tells it.

choices.text: Ask what she studied, and listen

effects.log: It is a long story, and it takes you to the far bank.

events.text: A pupil of {sda4_school} who never spoke to you, and whom you never quite noticed, stops you at the gate on your last morning and presses a carved wooden bird into your palm. It is crooked and quite ugly. They say they made it the first week and have been unable to give it to anyone since. They walk away quickly.

choices.text: Keep the bird on your windowsill

effects.log: It stays there for decades. Visitors ask about it.

choices.text: Carve one of your own, and send it back with the carrier

effects.log: The carrier takes it, grumbling. A reply comes in a month.

events.text: A boy of about twelve stands at your gate holding a note from {sda4_school}. It asks for a favour, in the school's careful hand: a letter delivered to a certain widow two valleys over. He will go with you if you like, he says; he knows the way. It is a long walk, and you suspect the letter is not merely a letter.

choices.text: Walk the two valleys with the boy and deliver it

effects.log: The widow reads it at the door, and sits down on the step. You wait until she can speak.

choices.text: Send the boy back with a coin and an apology

effects.log: He takes the coin with grave politeness. The letter goes with him.

events.text: A mortal sculptor is brought to {sda4_school} to carve the face of a god no one remembers, and the pupils are told to guess whose. The clay takes shape slowly: a broad brow, a patient mouth. By the third day half the class swears it is their own patron. The sculptor says nothing and keeps shaving the cheek.

choices.text: Study the face against the old hymn-books until it names itself

effects.log: It is a god of ferry-crossings, long forgotten. The sculptor weeps quietly when you say so.

choices.text: Insist loudly that it is your patron and dare anyone to deny it

effects.log: Nobody dares. The sculptor adds the patron nose, out of politeness.

choices.text: Ask the sculptor in private who sat for the face

effects.log: A dying ferryman, long ago. You keep it to yourself, and are trusted for it.
